theory.overview: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are one of the most exciting developments in deep learning, enabling AI to create realistic images, music, and even text. GANs consist of two neural networks—a Generator and a Discriminator—locked in an adversarial game. The Generator creates fake data trying to fool the Discriminator, while the Discriminator learns to distinguish real from fake. This competition drives both networks to improve, eventually producing remarkably realistic synthetic data.

sections.title: The Adversarial Game
sections.content: GANs frame generation as a two-player zero-sum game. The Generator (G) takes random noise and produces fake samples. The Discriminator (D) receives both real data and G's fakes, outputting a probability that each sample is real.
sections.minimaxObjective: min_G max_D V(D,G) = E[log D(x)] + E[log(1-D(G(z)))]
sections.intuition: D wants to maximize its accuracy (log D(x) high for real, log(1-D(G(z))) high for fake). G wants to minimize D's accuracy on its fakes—making D(G(z)) approach 1.

sections.title: Generator Architecture
sections.content: The Generator transforms a latent noise vector z into a realistic data sample. For images, it typically uses transposed convolutions (deconvolutions) to upsample from low to high resolution.
structure: Input: Random noise z ~ N(0,I), typically 100-512 dimensions
Hidden layers: Transposed convolutions + Batch Norm + ReLU
Output layer: Tanh or sigmoid for pixel values
Progressive growing: Start low-res, progressively add layers
sections.trainingGoal: Make D(G(z)) as close to 1 as possible—fooling the discriminator

sections.title: Discriminator Architecture
sections.content: The Discriminator is a standard CNN classifier. It outputs a single probability (real vs fake) and must become increasingly sophisticated as G improves.
structure: Downsampling through strided convolutions or pooling
sections.challenge: Must not become too good too fast, or G gets no useful gradients

sections.title: Training Dynamics
sections.content: GAN training is notoriously unstable. The balance between G and D is delicate—if D is too good, G gets vanishing gradients. If D is too weak, G receives poor feedback.

problems.name: Vanishing Gradients
problems.solution: Use Wasserstein loss or feature matching

problems.name: Mode Collapse
problems.cause: G finds limited variety that always fools D

sections.content: cGANs allow controlled generation by conditioning both G and D on additional information—class labels, text descriptions, or other images.
sections.modification: Concatenate condition vector to both z (input to G) and image (input to D)

sections.title: Applications & Impact
sections.content: GANs have enabled breakthroughs across creative and technical domains.

Face generation, age progression, expression editing

keyConcepts.name: Adversarial Training
keyConcepts.description: Two networks compete, driving each other to improve without direct supervision on generated data.
keyConcepts.analogy: Like a forger and an art detective—the forger improves as the detective gets better at spotting fakes

keyConcepts.name: Latent Space
keyConcepts.description: The noise vector z that G transforms into data. Points in this space map to generated samples.
keyConcepts.property: Smooth interpolation between points produces semantically meaningful transitions

keyConcepts.name: Mode Collapse
keyConcepts.description: G learns to produce only a few types of samples that consistently fool D, losing diversity.
keyConcepts.solution: Minibatch discrimination, experience replay, or architectural changes

keyConcepts.name: Wasserstein Distance
keyConcepts.description: Earth mover's distance—measures how much 'work' to transform one distribution to another.
keyConcepts.advantage: Provides meaningful gradients even when D is confident

complexity.generator: Similar to decoder in VAE—upsampling network
complexity.trainingTime: Long—needs careful balancing, often 2-10× longer than standard classification

practiceProblems.title: Generator Output Shape
practiceProblems.description: If G takes a 100-dim noise vector and generates 64×64 RGB images, how many output neurons?
practiceProblems.explanation: Each pixel has 3 color channels (R, G, B). The final layer of G must output values for every pixel position and channel.

practiceProblems.title: Minimax Game
practiceProblems.description: At convergence, what value should D(x) approach for both real and fake? Why?
practiceProblems.answer: 0.5—D cannot distinguish real from fake, so it random guesses. This is the Nash equilibrium.
practiceProblems.explanation: When G is perfect, P(fake) = P(real), so optimal D outputs P(real|x) = 0.5. At this point, neither can improve by unilateral change.

practiceProblems.title: Mode Collapse
practiceProblems.description: Your GAN generates faces, but all outputs look like the same person. What's happening?
practiceProblems.answer: Mode collapse—G found a single output that reliably fools D. It stopped exploring the full distribution.
practiceProblems.explanation: G has discovered a 'safe zone'—one mode of the data distribution that D accepts. Solutions: minibatch discrimination (D sees multiple samples), unrolled GANs (G anticipates D's response), or architectural diversity enforcement.

practiceProblems.title: Wasserstein vs Standard
practiceProblems.description: When D becomes too confident (D(x)≈1, D(G(z))≈0), what happens to G's gradients in standard GAN vs WGAN?
practiceProblems.answer: Standard GAN: vanishing gradients (log(1-D(G(z)))) saturates). WGAN: meaningful gradients (linear distance to optimality).
practiceProblems.explanation: In standard GAN, if D is perfect, loss saturates and G gets no signal. WGAN uses Wasserstein distance which is continuous and provides gradients even when distributions don't overlap.

practiceProblems.title: Conditional GAN
practiceProblems.description: Design a cGAN architecture for text-to-image synthesis.
practiceProblems.answer: Text encoder (RNN/Transformer) → sentence embedding. Concatenate with z → G produces image. D receives (image, text) pairs—learns joint distribution.
practiceProblems.explanation: Both G and D must be conditioned on text. G needs text to know what to generate. D needs text to verify semantic alignment. StackGAN approaches this hierarchically—sketch first, then details.

practiceProblems.title: Training Schedule
practiceProblems.description: Should you train D and G equally? If not, what's the typical ratio and why?
practiceProblems.answer: Often k:1 ratio (e.g., 5:1 or 1:1). D usually trained more initially to provide good signal, then balanced or G trained more.
practiceProblems.explanation: If D is too weak, G gets poor feedback. If D is too strong, G gets vanishing gradients. Progressive schedules: start with D-heavy, transition to balanced. Some use adaptive schedules based on D's accuracy.
hints: D needs to be good but not perfect

codeExample.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim

class Generator(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, latent_dim=100, img_size=28, channels=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.img_size = img_size
        self.channels = channels
        
        # For 28x28 MNIST: start 7x7, upsample twice
        self.model = nn.Sequential(
            # Input: latent_dim → 128 channels, 7x7
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(latent_dim, 128, 7, 1, 0),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(128),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            
            # 7x7 → 14x14
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(128, 64, 4, 2, 1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(64),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            
            # 14x14 → 28x28
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, channels, 4, 2, 1),
            nn.Tanh()  # Output [-1, 1]
        )
    
    def forward(self, z):
        # z: (batch, latent_dim) → (batch, latent_dim, 1, 1)
        z = z.view(z.size(0), z.size(1), 1, 1)
        img = self.model(z)
        return img

class Discriminator(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, img_size=28, channels=1):
        super().__init__()
        
        self.model = nn.Sequential(
            # 28x28 → 14x14
            nn.Conv2d(channels, 64, 4, 2, 1),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True),
            nn.Dropout2d(0.25),
            
            # 14x14 → 7x7
            nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 4, 2, 1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(128),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True),
            nn.Dropout2d(0.25),
            
            # Flatten and classify
            nn.Flatten(),
            nn.Linear(128 * 7 * 7, 1),
            nn.Sigmoid()
        )
    
    def forward(self, img):
        validity = self.model(img)
        return validity

def train_gan(generator, discriminator, dataloader, epochs=50, device='cuda'):
    """
    Basic GAN training loop
    """
    # Optimizers
    optimizer_G = optim.Adam(generator.parameters(), lr=0.0002, betas=(0.5, 0.999))
    optimizer_D = optim.Adam(discriminator.parameters(), lr=0.0002, betas=(0.5, 0.999))
    
    # Loss
    adversarial_loss = nn.BCELoss()
    
    generator.to(device)
    discriminator.to(device)
    
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        for i, (imgs, _) in enumerate(dataloader):
            batch_size = imgs.size(0)
            real_imgs = imgs.to(device)
            
            # Ground truths
            real_label = torch.ones(batch_size, 1).to(device)
            fake_label = torch.zeros(batch_size, 1).to(device)
            
            # ============= Train Generator =============
            optimizer_G.zero_grad()
            
            # Sample noise
            z = torch.randn(batch_size, 100).to(device)
            
            # Generate images
            gen_imgs = generator(z)
            
            # G wants D to believe these are real
            g_loss = adversarial_loss(discriminator(gen_imgs), real_label)
            
            g_loss.backward()
            optimizer_G.step()
            
            # ============= Train Discriminator =============
            optimizer_D.zero_grad()
            
            # D loss on real and fake
            real_loss = adversarial_loss(discriminator(real_imgs), real_label)
            fake_loss = adversarial_loss(discriminator(gen_imgs.detach()), fake_label)
            d_loss = (real_loss + fake_loss) / 2
            
            d_loss.backward()
            optimizer_D.step()
            
            if i % 100 == 0:
                print(f"Epoch {epoch}/{epochs} Batch {i}/{len(dataloader)} "
                      f"D_loss: {d_loss.item():.4f} G_loss: {g_loss.item():.4f}")

# Wasserstein GAN improvements
class WassersteinGAN:
    """
    Key changes for more stable training:
    1. Remove sigmoid from D (now outputs raw scores)
    2. Use Wasserstein loss instead of cross-entropy
    3. Weight clipping or gradient penalty
    4. Train D more than G
    """
    def wasserstein_loss(self, d_output, target_real):
        if target_real:
            return -torch.mean(d_output)  # Maximize D(x)
        else:
            return torch.mean(d_output)   # Minimize D(G(z))
    
    def gradient_penalty(self, discriminator, real_imgs, fake_imgs):
        """WGAN-GP: penalize deviation from unit gradient norm"""
        alpha = torch.rand(real_imgs.size(0), 1, 1, 1).to(real_imgs.device)
        interpolates = (alpha * real_imgs + (1 - alpha) * fake_imgs).requires_grad_(True)
        
        d_interpolates = discriminator(interpolates)
        gradients = torch.autograd.grad(
            outputs=d_interpolates,
            inputs=interpolates,
            grad_outputs=torch.ones_like(d_interpolates),
            create_graph=True,
            retain_graph=True
        )[0]
        
        gradients = gradients.view(gradients.size(0), -1)
        gradient_penalty = ((gradients.norm(2, dim=1) - 1) ** 2).mean()
        return gradient_penalty

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== GAN Architecture Summary ===")
    G = Generator(latent_dim=100, img_size=28, channels=1)
    D = Discriminator(img_size=28, channels=1)
    
    # Count parameters
    g_params = sum(p.numel() for p in G.parameters())
    d_params = sum(p.numel() for p in D.parameters())
    
    print(f"Generator parameters: {g_params:,}")
    print(f"Discriminator parameters: {d_params:,}")
    print(f"Total: {g_params + d_params:,}")
    
    # Test forward pass
    z = torch.randn(16, 100)
    fake_imgs = G(z)
    d_output = D(fake_imgs)
    
    print(f"\nGenerator output shape: {fake_imgs.shape}")
    print(f"Discriminator output shape: {d_output.shape}")
    print(f"D(fake) range: [{d_output.min():.3f}, {d_output.max():.3f}]")
